references.text: The Pharisees and the scribes asked the same question: 'Who is this who forgives sins, except God alone?' When Jesus forgave the paralytic man's sins, they reacted in the same way as the guests at the table in Luke 7:49.
The immediate context where Jesus declares forgiveness of the woman's sins, which triggers the reaction from the dinner guests about who this is that even forgives sins.

In Mark's parallel account of the healing of the paralytic man, the scribes ask the same question in their hearts: 'Who can forgive sins except one, that is God?' The same reaction to Jesus' authority to forgive sins.
The scribes said that Jesus was blaspheming God when he told the paralytic, 'Your sins are forgiven.' The same kind of resistance to Jesus' authority to forgive sins as we see in Luke 7:49.

God alone is the one who blots out transgressions for his own sake and does not remember sins. The guests' question in Luke 7:49 reflects this theological conviction that forgiveness of sins is God's sovereign right.
The disciples asked a similar question: 'Who is this?' when Jesus calmed the storm. The question about Jesus' identity is a recurring theme in the Gospel of Luke, triggered by his divine actions.
The people asked, 'What kind of word is this?' when Jesus cast out an unclean spirit. The same pattern of wonder and questioning about Jesus' identity and authority.
